question: In monsoon season, a 9-year-old boy has 5 days of high fever with severe headache, retro-orbital pain, myalgia, and a petechial rash appearing as fever defervesces. A 6-year-old girl has sudden fever with severe joint pain and a maculopapular rash. A 7-year-old presents with high spiking fever every 48 hours and rigors. Which pairing correctly matches child to disease?

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. Retro-orbital pain and petechial rash appearing at defervescence are characteristic of dengue, not chikungunya. Severe debilitating joint pain is the hallmark of chikungunya.

Correct. Dengue: fever + retro-orbital pain + myalgia + petechial rash at defervescence. Chikungunya: fever + severe incapacitating polyarthralgia + maculopapular rash. Malaria (P. vivax): periodic high spiking fever every 48 hours (tertian) + rigors + no rash. These are the distinguishing clinical signatures during monsoon season in India.
Incorrect. Periodic 48-hour fever cycles with rigors is the hallmark of malaria (P. vivax tertian pattern), not chikungunya. Retro-orbital pain and petechial rash are dengue features.
Incorrect. Severe joint pain (arthralgia) and maculopapular rash describe chikungunya, not malaria. Malaria has periodic fever with rigors, not prominent joint involvement.

overallFeedback.feedback: Review the clinical presentations of vector-borne fevers. Key differentiators: dengue has retro-orbital pain and petechial rash; chikungunya has severe joint pain; malaria has periodic 48-hour fever cycles (vivax) or 72-hour cycles (falciparum) with rigors.
Correct. Dengue = retro-orbital pain + petechiae at defervescence. Chikungunya = incapacitating polyarthralgia + maculopapular rash. Malaria (P. vivax) = 48-hour cyclic fever with rigors.
